nameStory: The sooty shearwater gets its name from its dark, soot-colored plumage that looks like it's been dusted with charcoal from a chimney. The 'shearwater' part comes from these seabirds' amazing ability to 'shear' or glide just inches above the water's surface, using the air currents created by waves to fly effortlessly for hours.
description: The sooty shearwater is a medium-large seabird that's built for life on the open ocean. These dark, cigar-shaped birds have long, narrow wings perfect for gliding over waves and a sturdy build about the size of a small gull. They're masters of oceanic flight, spending most of their lives far from shore riding wind currents above the waves. In New Zealand, they're known as tītī and are culturally important to the Māori people.

idTips.label: Overall coloration
idTips.description: Uniformly dark sooty brown or grayish-brown all over, looking like they've been rolled in ash or charcoal dust

idTips.label: Wing shape
idTips.description: Very long, narrow wings held stiffly straight out from the body, appearing almost cross-like when gliding

idTips.label: Flight pattern
idTips.description: Glides low over waves with minimal wing flapping, occasionally banking sharply to show silvery underwing patches

idTips.label: Body shape
idTips.description: Streamlined, torpedo-shaped body with a relatively large head and straight, dark bill

idTips.label: Underwing markings
idTips.description: Pale silvery-white patches visible on the underwings when banking, contrasting with the otherwise dark plumage

habitat: Found exclusively in offshore waters of the North Atlantic, typically many miles from the New England coast. Look for them from whale-watching boats, ferries, or during pelagic birding trips in deep, cold waters over the continental shelf. They prefer areas where ocean currents bring nutrient-rich waters to the surface.

seasonality.spring: Begin arriving in New England waters in late spring as they start their incredible migration from the Southern Hemisphere. Numbers are generally low but increasing through the season.
seasonality.summer: Peak abundance occurs during summer months when they're most likely to be spotted from boats. This is the best time for whale-watching trips that might encounter these ocean wanderers.
seasonality.fall: Still present in good numbers through early fall before beginning their journey back south. Late summer to early fall offers some of the most reliable sightings.
seasonality.winter: Absent from New England waters as they return to breeding grounds in the Southern Hemisphere, completing one of the longest migrations in the animal kingdom.

funFact: Sooty shearwaters make one of the longest migrations of any animal on Earth, traveling roughly 40,000 miles annually in a figure-eight pattern across the entire Pacific Ocean - that's like flying around the Earth one and a half times every single year!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with the larger Great Shearwater, but sooty shearwaters are uniformly dark all over while Great Shearwaters have a distinctive white collar and white patches on the rump. Think 'sooty = solid dark' to remember the difference.
contextualKnowledge: These birds are known as 'muttonbirds' in New Zealand and Australia, not because they taste like mutton, but because early European settlers thought their meat was a substitute for sheep meat. The Māori name 'tītī' reflects their cultural importance as a traditional food source that's still sustainably harvested today.
compareHints: Compared to its close relative the Great Shearwater, the sooty shearwater is smaller, uniformly dark, and lacks the Great Shearwater's distinctive white collar and rump patches. While Great Shearwaters have a more contrasting black-and-white pattern, sooty shearwaters are essentially monochrome except for those silvery underwing flashes.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Great Shearwaters are larger and cleaner-looking than their close relative, the Sooty Shearwater, which appears uniformly dark brown all over.
